## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Anabhiratijātaka* (Ja 65) is a narrative text preserved in the first volume of the Pali *Jātaka* collection [Fausböll 1877]. Set at Jetavana, the frame story relates that a lay disciple (*upāsaka*) was overcome with emotional distress after discovering his wife's infidelity and misconduct, which caused him to neglect visiting the Buddha for over a week [Fausböll 1877]. In response, the Buddha consoles the man and recounts a past-life story illustrating that wise individuals should not give way to anger over the frailties of women [Lakshmi Narasu 1907; Burlingame 1921].

The core verse of the Jātaka begins with the opening *Yathā nadī ca pantho ca* ("Just as rivers and pathways..."), comparing womankind to highways, rivers, court-yards, and inns that are accessible to all alike [Fausböll 1877; Lakshmi Narasu 1907]. In the conclusion (*samodhāna*), the Buddha explains that the married couple of the past were the same lay couple in the present, while the Bodhisatta was the learned teacher (*ācariyabrāhmaṇa*) who imparted the teaching; upon hearing the discourse, the lay brother attains the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*) [Fausböll 1877]. This story is also referenced in the *Dhammapada* commentary in connection with a husband humiliated by his unfaithful wife [Burlingame 1921].

 The text should not be confused with a homonymous discourse, the *Anabhiratijātaka* numbered as Jātaka 185 in the collection.
